report.summary: Fitness landscapes in program search exhibit high neutrality and ruggedness. Most mutations are neutral or fatal due to code redundancy, syntactic invalidity, or extreme behavioral disruption. Operator design should minimize lethality and leverage neutrality, e.g., via semantic preservation and structural constraints.

handoff.suggestion: Fitness landscape analysis for program search reveals pervasive neutrality and ruggedness, with profound implications for operator design. Neutrality arises from introns, equivalent code fragments, and behavioral redundancy: studies in genetic programming (GP) report that 60–80% of single-point mutations are either neutral or lethal (Harper, 2010, uncertain; Luke, 2000, observed similar rates for crossover). This high neutrality buffers populations against disruptive change but also slows adaptation. Lethal mutations stem from syntax errors, infinite loops, or catastrophic semantic breaks, often exceeding 30% of all mutants in unconstrained GP (Banzhaf et al., 1998). Ruggedness results from epistasis and discontinuity: small genotypic changes can cause large fitness swings, creating deceptive landscapes with many local optima (Kinnear, 1994). These features imply that traditional operators—random subtree mutation or crossover—are inefficient. Instead, operators should respect syntactic and semantic locality. Grammar-based approaches (Whigham, 1996) reduce lethality by constraining mutation to valid programs. Semantic operators (Moraglio et al., 2012) explicitly target behavioral change, improving local search. Neutrality can be exploited via neutral drift to escape local optima (Miller & Thomson, 2000, in Cartesian GP). The most actionable step: adopt semantics-aware mutation operators that maintain syntactic validity and enforce behavioral diversity, e.g., by using type-guided subtree replacements or software transplantation (Barr et al., 2015). Such operators dramatically lower the lethal mutation rate and focus search on meaningful variations.
